lessons.title: Understanding Broiler Health in African Production Systems
lessons.body: Broiler production in Africa is a business where health is money. Every sick bird reduces feed conversion, slows growth, increases medication costs, and lowers your profit margin. In many African countries, small and medium-scale broiler farmers operate with limited veterinary support, inconsistent electricity, variable water quality, and high heat stress. This lesson gives you a practical foundation for keeping broilers healthy from day-old chick to market weight. First, understand that broiler health is not only about treating disease. It is about prevention, observation, biosecurity, nutrition, water, ventilation, and stress management. A healthy broiler flock eats well, drinks well, moves actively, has bright eyes, clean feathers, and uniform growth. When you see birds huddling, panting, sitting, or making abnormal sounds, act immediately. In Africa, the most common broiler health challenges include Newcastle disease, infectious bursal disease (Gumboro), infectious bronchitis, coccidiosis, chronic respiratory disease, colibacillosis, fowl typhoid, and heat stress. External parasites such as mites and lice also reduce performance. Mycotoxins in feed, especially aflatoxins, are a major hidden cause of poor health and immune suppression. Your first business decision is sourcing chicks from a reputable hatchery. Cheap chicks from unknown sources often carry disease or have poor immunity. Buy from hatcheries that vaccinate against Marek's disease and provide health records. Day-old chicks should be active, have dry navels, bright eyes, and uniform size. Place them in a clean, pre-warmed brooder with feed and water available immediately. The first 7 days determine flock uniformity and survival. Biosecurity is your cheapest insurance. Limit visitors, use footbaths with disinfectant at every entrance, keep different age groups separate, and control rodents and wild birds. In many African farms, the same boots and clothes move between houses. Stop this. Use dedicated boots and overalls per house. Clean and disinfect feeders and drinkers daily. Remove wet litter immediately because wet litter causes coccidiosis, footpad dermatitis, and ammonia build-up. Ammonia damages the respiratory tract and opens the door to secondary infections. Water quality is critical. Broilers drink about 1.6 to 2 times more water than feed. If water is dirty or has high bacterial load, birds will get sick. Test your water source, clean tanks weekly, and use chlorine or other approved sanitizers at correct levels. Never medicate through dirty water. Heat stress is the biggest silent killer in African broiler production. Temperatures above 30 degrees Celsius reduce feed intake, growth, and immunity. Provide enough ventilation, use fans, open side curtains, increase roof insulation, and give cool water. Add electrolytes and vitamin C during hot periods. Avoid handling birds during the hottest part of the day. Feed quality directly affects health. Buy feed from reputable millers or mix your own with correct protein, energy, vitamins, and minerals. Never use mouldy maize or groundnut cake. Store feed on pallets in a dry, ventilated place. Use mould inhibitors or toxin binders when risk is high. Aflatoxin contamination is common in warm, humid African climates and causes liver damage, poor growth, and immune suppression. Vaccination is the backbone of disease prevention, but it only works if birds are healthy, vaccines are handled correctly, and the schedule is followed. This module will cover vaccination in detail in later lessons. For now, remember that vaccines do not replace biosecurity, good nutrition, and clean water. They work together. Record keeping is a business tool. Keep daily records of mortality, feed intake, water intake, temperature, and any symptoms. Mortality above 0.5 percent per day after the first week is a warning. A sudden drop in water intake often means disease or heat stress. Weigh a sample of birds weekly to track growth. If growth is below breed standard, investigate health, feed, or environment. Common diseases and signs: Newcastle disease causes gasping, coughing, twisted neck, and high mortality. Gumboro causes watery droppings, depression, and immunosuppression. Infectious bronchitis causes sneezing, rales, and poor egg quality in breeders. Coccidiosis causes bloody droppings, pale birds, and poor growth. Chronic respiratory disease causes snickering, nasal discharge, and swollen eyes. Colibacillosis causes lethargy, diarrhoea, and high mortality. Fowl typhoid causes yellow diarrhoea, pale combs, and sudden death. If you suspect a disease, isolate sick birds, consult a veterinarian, and do not sell medicated birds without observing withdrawal periods. Treat only with approved drugs and correct dosage. Overuse of antibiotics leads to resistance and residue problems. In Africa, access to veterinary services may be limited, so build a relationship with a local vet or extension officer before problems occur. Keep a simple medicine kit with disinfectants, electrolytes, vitamins, and common treatments. Store vaccines and medicines in a refrigerator or cool box with ice packs. Power cuts are common, so have a backup plan. Finally, think like a business. Healthy broilers reach market weight in 5 to 7 weeks with good feed conversion. Sick broilers take longer, eat more, and sell for less. Every naira, shilling, cedi, or rand spent on prevention returns more than money spent on treatment. Your goal is not to react to disease but to create an environment where disease cannot easily enter or spread. In the next lessons, you will learn specific vaccination schedules, vaccine handling, and disease-specific control measures for African conditions.

lessons.title: Vaccination Principles and Vaccine Handling for Broilers
lessons.body: Vaccination is one of the most cost-effective tools in broiler production, but only when done correctly. In Africa, many vaccination failures happen not because the vaccine is bad but because it was stored, handled, or administered wrongly. This lesson teaches you the principles of vaccination and practical vaccine handling for broiler flocks. First, understand what a vaccine does. A vaccine exposes the bird to a weakened or killed form of a disease organism. The bird's immune system responds by producing antibodies and memory cells. If the real disease attacks later, the bird can fight it off. For broilers, the goal is to protect birds during their short life, usually 5 to 7 weeks. Vaccines must be given at the right age, right dose, and right route. There are different types of vaccines. Live vaccines contain weakened live organisms. They usually give strong, fast immunity but must be handled carefully. Killed vaccines contain dead organisms and often need adjuvants. They give slower but longer immunity. Recombinant vaccines use parts of organisms and are very safe. In broiler production, common live vaccines include Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis, and Gumboro. Killed vaccines are less common in broilers because of the short cycle. The cold chain is the most important part of vaccine handling. Most vaccines must be kept between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius. Freezing can damage some vaccines, especially Gumboro and Newcastle live vaccines. Heat destroys vaccines quickly. In African conditions, where temperatures can exceed 35 degrees Celsius and electricity is unreliable, you must plan carefully. Use a dedicated vaccine fridge, not a fridge for food or drinks. Keep a thermometer inside. If power is unstable, use a cool box with ice packs or a solar fridge. Never store vaccines in a car boot or on a motorbike in the sun. When transporting vaccines, use a cool box with ice packs and a thermometer. Do not put vaccines directly on ice because they can freeze. Wrap them in paper or cloth. Check the temperature when you arrive. If the vaccine is warm or frozen, do not use it. Record the temperature. Reconstitution is another critical step. Live vaccines come as a freeze-dried powder in a vial and a diluent in another vial. Reconstitute only when you are ready to use. Use the correct diluent supplied by the manufacturer. Do not use water, saline, or other liquids unless approved. Use a clean syringe to draw the diluent and inject it into the vaccine vial. Mix gently. Do not shake vigorously because it can damage the vaccine. Use the vaccine within 1 to 2 hours. Keep it cool during use. If you are vaccinating many birds, keep the vaccine vial in a cool container with ice packs. Do not leave it in the sun. Administration routes for broilers include drinking water, eye drop, nose drop, and injection. Drinking water vaccination is common for Newcastle and infectious bronchitis in large flocks. It is less stressful but requires careful preparation. First, withdraw water for 1 to 2 hours before vaccination so birds are thirsty. Use clean water without chlorine or disinfectants because they kill the vaccine. If your water has chlorine, add skim milk powder or a commercial vaccine stabilizer. Calculate the correct amount of water based on the number of birds and their age. A common rule is 10 to 20 millilitres per bird, but follow the vaccine manufacturer's instructions. Mix the vaccine in a clean container and distribute it quickly to drinkers. Make sure every bird gets a drink. Walk through the house to encourage birds to drink. Remove any remaining vaccine water after 1 to 2 hours and clean the drinkers. Eye drop and nose drop vaccination give more precise doses. Use a dropper to place one drop in the eye or nostril. This route is common for Newcastle and infectious bronchitis in small flocks or when water quality is poor. It requires handling each bird, which is stressful but effective. Injection routes include subcutaneous and intramuscular. Subcutaneous injection is usually given in the neck. Intramuscular injection is given in the breast muscle. Use a short needle and change it regularly. Do not inject into the bone or internal organs. Killed vaccines are often given by injection. For broilers, injection is less common but may be used for some diseases. Hygiene during vaccination is essential. Use clean equipment. Boil syringes and needles before use. Do not use disinfectants on equipment that will contact live vaccines because they can kill the vaccine. Use separate equipment for different vaccines. Wash hands before and after. Handle birds gently to reduce stress. Stress reduces vaccine response. Do not vaccinate sick birds. Do not vaccinate during extreme heat. Do not vaccinate birds that are already showing disease signs. If a disease outbreak is ongoing, consult a veterinarian before vaccinating. Vaccinate early in the morning or late in the evening when temperatures are cooler. Give vitamins and electrolytes before and after vaccination to reduce stress. Avoid mixing vaccines unless the manufacturer says it is safe. Some vaccines can be given together, but others cannot. Read the label. Record every vaccination. Write down the date, vaccine name, batch number, expiry date, route, dose, number of birds, and who did it. This record helps you trace problems and plan future flocks. Common vaccination mistakes in Africa include using expired vaccines, storing vaccines in wrong temperatures, using chlorinated water for drinking water vaccination, mixing too much vaccine at once, vaccinating sick birds, and using wrong routes. Each mistake can cause vaccine failure and disease outbreak. Vaccine failure can also happen if the vaccine is not effective against the local field strain. Some diseases have different strains. Work with your veterinarian to choose vaccines that match local challenges. Also, remember that vaccination does not give immediate immunity. It takes 5 to 14 days for full protection. During this time, biosecurity must be strong. Maternal antibodies from the parent flock can also interfere with vaccines. That is why timing is important. For example, Gumboro vaccine is often given when maternal antibodies have dropped enough to allow the vaccine to work. Your vaccination schedule should be based on local disease pressure, breed, and veterinary advice. A typical broiler schedule in Africa may include Marek's at hatchery, Newcastle and infectious bronchitis at day 1 or day 7, Gumboro at day 10 to 14, and Newcastle booster at day 21 to 28. But this varies. Some farms also vaccinate against fowl pox, avian influenza, or other diseases depending on region. Do not copy a schedule blindly. Adapt it to your farm. Finally, treat vaccination as a business investment. A vial of vaccine may cost a small amount, but a disease outbreak can wipe out your entire flock and your profit. Train your workers. Demonstrate correct technique. Supervise. Check records. If you do all these things, vaccination will protect your birds and your income.

lessons.title: A Practical Broiler Vaccination Schedule for African Farms
lessons.body: A vaccination schedule is a plan that tells you which vaccine to give, at what age, by which route, and for which disease. In Africa, broiler production faces different disease pressures depending on country, region, season, and farm biosecurity. There is no single schedule that fits every farm. However, this lesson gives you a practical, adaptable schedule that many African broiler farmers use successfully. Always confirm with your local veterinarian or extension officer. The first vaccine is usually given at the hatchery. Marek's disease vaccine is given to day-old chicks at the hatchery, usually by injection. If your hatchery does not vaccinate against Marek's, ask why. Marek's causes tumours, paralysis, and death. It is very common in some areas. You cannot easily vaccinate for Marek's on the farm because it must be given very early. So buy chicks from a hatchery that vaccinates. At day 1, some farms give Newcastle disease and infectious bronchitis vaccine by eye drop or nose drop. This is common in areas with high Newcastle pressure. The vaccine is often a combined vaccine. If your hatchery already gave this, do not repeat unnecessarily. Check with your supplier. At day 7, many farms give Newcastle disease and infectious bronchitis vaccine by drinking water or eye drop. This is a common first farm vaccination. Use a live vaccine. Withdraw water for 1 to 2 hours before vaccination. Use clean water with skim milk powder or stabilizer. Give the correct dose. At day 10 to 14, give infectious bursal disease (Gumboro) vaccine by drinking water. The exact timing depends on maternal antibody levels. If you can, test maternal antibodies or follow the hatchery's advice. In high-risk areas, some farms give a first Gumboro vaccine at day 10 and a second at day 18 to 21. Gumboro is a major cause of immunosuppression in African broilers. It damages the bursa of Fabricius, which is important for immune development. If birds get Gumboro, they become vulnerable to many other diseases. At day 18 to 21, give Newcastle disease booster by drinking water. This is important because Newcastle is endemic in many African countries. Some farms also give infectious bronchitis booster at this time. Use a live vaccine. Again, follow the cold chain and water preparation rules. At day 21 to 28, some farms give a second Gumboro vaccine if risk is high. Others give fowl pox vaccine if the disease is common in the area. Fowl pox is spread by mosquitoes and causes skin lesions and poor growth. It is more common in wet seasons. Fowl pox vaccine is given by wing web stab. It is not always needed in broilers because the cycle is short, but in high-risk areas it can be useful. At day 28 to 35, some farms give a final Newcastle booster. This depends on market age. If you sell at 5 weeks, you may not need it. If you sell at 7 weeks or later, it helps. Some farms also vaccinate against infectious bronchitis at this time. Other vaccines that may be used in specific situations include avian influenza, fowl cholera, and infectious coryza. Avian influenza is a serious disease and vaccination policies vary by country. Some countries do not allow avian influenza vaccination. Check your national regulations. Fowl cholera and infectious coryza are bacterial diseases. Vaccines exist but are not always used in broilers because of cost and short life. Antibiotics and management are often used instead. A sample schedule for a 6-week broiler flock in a moderate-risk African farm: Day 1 at hatchery: Marek's. Day 1 on farm: Newcastle plus infectious bronchitis by eye drop if not done at hatchery. Day 7: Newcastle plus infectious bronchitis by drinking water. Day 10 to 12: Gumboro by drinking water. Day 18 to 21: Newcastle booster by drinking water. Day 21 to 24: Gumboro booster if high risk. Day 28: Newcastle booster if selling after 6 weeks. This is only a guide. Adjust based on local disease history. If your area has frequent Newcastle outbreaks, you may need earlier and more frequent vaccination. If Gumboro is a problem, you may need to test maternal antibodies and time the vaccine precisely. If coccidiosis is a problem, you may use coccidiostats in feed or vaccines. Coccidiosis vaccines are available and are given by spray or drinking water at day 1 to 3. They are more common in some countries than others. Water quality affects vaccination success. If your water has high chlorine, it will kill live vaccines. Use skim milk powder at 2 to 3 grams per litre or a commercial stabilizer. If water is very dirty, use eye drop or nose drop instead of drinking water. Do not use metal containers for vaccine water because metal ions can damage vaccines. Use plastic containers. Do not use disinfectants in drinkers before vaccination. Rinse thoroughly. Heat stress reduces vaccine response. If you must vaccinate during hot weather, do it early morning or late evening. Give vitamins and electrolytes. Avoid vaccination during disease outbreaks unless advised by a vet. Do not vaccinate birds that are already sick. Record every vaccination. Keep a notebook or computer record. Include date, age, vaccine name, batch number, expiry date, route, dose, number of birds, and person who did it. This helps you identify problems and improve next cycle. Common problems with vaccination schedules in Africa include missing a vaccine because of supply issues, using expired vaccines, storing vaccines in a fridge that is off, using wrong diluent, vaccinating sick birds, and not recording. Plan ahead. Buy vaccines before you need them. Check expiry dates. Have a backup power source for the fridge. Train your workers. If you follow a good schedule and handle vaccines correctly, you will reduce disease and increase profit. Remember, vaccination is not a substitute for biosecurity. Keep visitors out. Clean and disinfect. Control rodents and wild birds. Provide good feed and water. Manage heat stress. A vaccinated flock in a dirty house can still get sick. A well-managed flock with good vaccination will perform well. Finally, work with your veterinarian. Disease patterns change. New strains appear. Regulations change. Your vet can help you adjust your schedule to your farm and your region. Do not rely on guesswork. Use records, observation, and professional advice.

lessons.title: Disease Prevention and Control in Broiler Flocks
lessons.body: Preventing disease is cheaper than treating it. In African broiler production, disease outbreaks can destroy your flock and your business within days. This lesson covers practical disease prevention and control measures that work in real farm conditions. Start with biosecurity. Biosecurity means keeping disease out and stopping it from spreading. It is the first line of defence. Every broiler farm should have a biosecurity plan. Write it down. Train your workers. Enforce it. Key biosecurity steps: limit visitors. Only essential people enter the farm. Keep a visitor log. Provide boots and overalls. Use footbaths with fresh disinfectant at every house entrance. Change disinfectant regularly because it loses strength. Keep different age groups in separate houses. Do not mix chicks and older birds. Control rodents and wild birds. They carry disease. Use traps, baits, and netting. Keep feed in closed containers. Clean up spilled feed. Remove dead birds immediately. Dispose of them properly by burning, burying, or composting. Do not throw dead birds in the bush or feed them to dogs. Disinfect the house between flocks. Remove all litter. Wash with detergent. Disinfect with an approved product. Let the house dry. Rest the house for at least 7 to 14 days. Use a different disinfectant for different flocks to prevent resistance. Control traffic. Vehicles can carry disease. Keep vehicles away from the poultry house. If a vehicle must enter, disinfect its wheels. Do not let traders walk through your houses. Sell birds at the gate or in a separate area. Water and feed hygiene are also critical. Clean and disinfect drinkers and feeders daily. Use clean water. Test water for bacteria and chemicals. Store water in clean tanks. Cover tanks. Do not let birds drink from puddles or dirty containers. Feed should be fresh and free of mould. Store feed on pallets. Keep feed room dry and ventilated. Use feed within 2 to 3 weeks. Do not use feed that is caked, discoloured, or smells musty. Mycotoxins are a major problem in Africa. They come from moulds in maize, groundnut, and other feed ingredients. Aflatoxin is the most dangerous. It causes liver damage, poor growth, immune suppression, and death. Use a toxin binder in feed when risk is high. Buy ingredients from trusted suppliers. Test if possible. Ventilation and temperature control prevent respiratory disease and heat stress. Broilers need fresh air without drafts. Ammonia levels should be below 20 parts per million. If your eyes sting when you enter the house, ammonia is too high. Increase ventilation. Remove wet litter. Add fresh litter. Use fans, vents, and curtains. In hot climates, use roof insulation, fans, foggers, and cool water. In cold weather, avoid drafts but keep air fresh. Stocking density affects health. Too many birds in a small space increases stress, disease spread, and litter problems. Follow breed recommendations. Usually 10 to 12 birds per square metre in open houses, or more in controlled environment houses. Provide enough feeders and drinkers. Birds should not crowd. If they crowd, some will not eat or drink enough. This leads to poor uniformity and disease. Vaccination is a key prevention tool. Follow the schedule. Handle vaccines correctly. But remember, vaccination does not replace management. A vaccinated bird in a dirty house can still get sick. Common diseases and control: Newcastle disease. Cause: virus. Signs: gasping, coughing, twisted neck, paralysis, high mortality. Control: vaccinate. Biosecurity. No treatment. Gumboro. Cause: virus. Signs: watery droppings, depression, ruffled feathers, immunosuppression. Control: vaccinate. Biosecurity. No specific treatment. Infectious bronchitis. Cause: virus. Signs: sneezing, rales, nasal discharge, poor growth. Control: vaccinate. Ventilation. Biosecurity. Coccidiosis. Cause: parasite. Signs: bloody droppings, pale birds, poor growth. Control: coccidiostats in feed or water. Coccidiosis vaccine. Clean, dry litter. Chronic respiratory disease. Cause: bacteria-like organisms. Signs: snickering, nasal discharge, swollen eyes. Control: antibiotics if bacterial. Improve ventilation. Reduce stress. Colibacillosis. Cause: bacteria. Signs: lethargy, diarrhoea, high mortality. Control: antibiotics. Clean water. Good hygiene. Fowl typhoid. Cause: bacteria. Signs: yellow diarrhoea, pale combs, sudden death. Control: antibiotics. Vaccination in some areas. Biosecurity. External parasites. Mites, lice, fleas. Control: insecticides. Clean houses. Treat birds. Internal parasites. Worms. Control: dewormers. Clean litter. Avoid overcrowding. Heat stress. Not a disease but a major killer. Signs: panting, wings out, lethargy, reduced feed intake. Control: ventilation, fans, cool water, electrolytes, vitamin C, shade, roof insulation. When disease strikes, act fast. Isolate sick birds. Consult a veterinarian. Do not guess. Use the correct drug at the correct dose for the correct duration. Observe withdrawal periods. Do not sell meat with drug residues. Record everything. If mortality is high, send samples to a laboratory. Many African countries have veterinary laboratories. Use them. Do not rely on neighbours' advice alone. After an outbreak, clean and disinfect thoroughly. Rest the house. Find out what went wrong. Fix it. Do not bring new chicks into a contaminated house. Common mistakes in African broiler disease control: poor biosecurity, dirty water, wet litter, overcrowding, heat stress, expired vaccines, wrong vaccine handling, overuse of antibiotics, no records, and delayed action. Each mistake costs money. Prevention is a business strategy. Healthy birds grow faster, convert feed better, and sell for higher prices. Sick birds cost you feed, medicine, labour, and lost sales. Invest in prevention. Train your workers. Keep records. Work with a vet. Use good quality inputs. Manage the environment. If you do these things, you will reduce disease and increase profit. Finally, remember that disease control is a daily habit, not a one-time event. Check your birds every morning and evening. Look at their behaviour, droppings, feed, and water intake. Act early. Small problems become big problems if ignored. Your attention is your best disease control tool.

lessons.title: Record Keeping, Monitoring, and Business Decisions for Broiler Health
lessons.body: Broiler health is not only a veterinary issue. It is a business issue. Every health decision affects your costs, your revenue, and your profit. This lesson teaches you how to use record keeping and monitoring to make better business decisions for broiler health in African conditions. Start with daily records. You need to know what is happening in your flock every day. Record mortality. Count dead birds every morning and evening. Write down the number and possible cause. A sudden increase in mortality is a red flag. Record feed intake. Weigh or estimate feed given each day. A drop in feed intake can mean disease, heat stress, or poor feed quality. Record water intake. Water intake often changes before other signs appear. A sudden drop in water intake can mean disease or heat stress. A sudden increase can mean diarrhoea or fever. Record temperature and humidity. Use a thermometer and hygrometer. Record morning, afternoon, and evening readings. Record any symptoms you see. Coughing, sneezing, diarrhoea, lameness, swollen eyes, twisted neck. Record treatments given. Drug name, dose, route, date, withdrawal period. Record vaccinations. Vaccine name, batch number, expiry date, route, dose, date, who did it. Record body weight. Weigh a sample of birds weekly. Use a scale. Weigh at least 10 birds from different parts of the house. Calculate average weight. Compare to breed standard. If below standard, investigate. Record feed conversion ratio. This is feed consumed divided by weight gained. Good broiler feed conversion is usually 1.5 to 1.8. If it is higher, your birds are eating more but growing less. This means disease, poor feed, or poor environment. Record costs. Feed, chicks, vaccines, medicines, labour, electricity, water, litter, transport. Record revenue. Number of birds sold, weight, price per kilogram. Calculate profit per flock. These records help you see patterns. Maybe mortality is always high in the first week. Maybe feed conversion is poor in hot months. Maybe a certain vaccine always causes a reaction. With records, you can fix problems and improve. Monitoring is more than records. It is observation. Walk through your houses every day. Look at the birds. Are they active? Are they eating? Are they drinking? Are they panting? Are they huddling? Look at the litter. Is it dry? Is it caked? Look at the droppings. Are they normal? Are they watery? Are they bloody? Look at the feeders and drinkers. Are they clean? Are they full? Look at the walls and roof. Are there cracks? Are there rodents? Are there wild birds? Listen to the birds. Do you hear coughing, sneezing, or snickering? Smell the air. Is there ammonia? If you see or smell something wrong, act immediately. Do not wait. In Africa, many farmers delay action because they hope the problem will go away. It rarely does. Early action saves birds and money. Use a simple scoring system. For example, score litter dryness from 1 to 5. Score bird activity from 1 to 5. Score air quality from 1 to 5. Write these scores daily. This helps you track changes over time. If scores drop, investigate. Use a mortality chart. Plot daily mortality on a graph. A spike shows a problem. Use a growth chart. Plot weekly weights against breed standard. If your birds are below standard, find out why. Use a feed and water chart. Plot daily intake. A sudden change is a warning. These tools do not require expensive software. A notebook and pen work. A whiteboard on the farm wall works. A simple spreadsheet on a phone or computer works. The key is consistency. Record every day. Review every week. Make decisions based on data, not guesswork. Business decisions from health records: When to sell. If mortality is rising and birds are not growing, selling early may reduce losses. If birds are healthy and growing well, selling at target weight gives best profit. When to cull. Sick birds that will not recover should be culled humanely. They consume feed and may spread disease. Culling reduces losses. When to treat. If you see early signs of disease, treat quickly. But do not treat blindly. Use the right drug. If you do not know the cause, consult a vet. When to vaccinate. Follow your schedule. If disease is in the area, consider earlier vaccination. If vaccine supply is a problem, plan ahead. When to change feed. If feed conversion is poor and health is good, the feed may be the problem. Change to a better feed or adjust the ration. When to improve housing. If heat stress or ammonia is a recurring problem, invest in ventilation, insulation, or better litter management. When to train workers. If mistakes happen often, train again. Show them the records. Explain why each task matters. When to borrow or invest. If records show that a small investment in a fan, a fridge, or a water filter will reduce mortality and improve growth, calculate the return. Many health improvements pay for themselves within one or two flocks. Common record keeping mistakes in Africa: not recording, recording only mortality, recording on loose papers that get lost, not reviewing records, not sharing records with workers, and not using records to make decisions. Fix these mistakes. Keep a farm diary. Keep a flock file. Keep vaccination records. Keep treatment records. Keep financial records. At the end of each flock, do a flock review. What went well? What went wrong? What will you change next time? Write it down. Share it with your team. Use it to plan the next flock. Health and business are connected. A healthy flock is a profitable flock. A sick flock is a costly flock. By keeping good records and monitoring closely, you can detect problems early, act fast, and protect your investment. You can also prove to buyers, lenders, and insurers that your farm is well managed. This opens doors to better markets and financing. In Africa, broiler production is a growing business. Demand for chicken is rising. But competition is also rising. Farmers who manage health well and keep good records will succeed. Farmers who ignore health and records will struggle. Choose to be a professional broiler farmer. Use records. Monitor daily. Make decisions based on facts. Train your workers. Work with your vet. Invest in prevention. Your birds will reward you with fast growth, low mortality, and good profit. Remember, the goal is not just to keep birds alive. The goal is to produce healthy, heavy birds at the lowest cost per kilogram. Records and monitoring help you do that. Start today. Even a simple notebook is better than nothing. Write down what you see. Review it. Act on it. Your business will grow.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Health Records, Cost Benchmarks, and Decision Triggers for African Broiler Farms

This Practical Reference lesson supports the module on broiler health by translating flock health observations into business decisions. In African production systems, where margins are often thin and input costs volatile, the difference between profit and loss frequently comes down to how quickly a farmer detects a health problem and how decisively they respond. The aim here is simple: give you the reference tables, benchmarks, and checklists you need to act on health data rather than merely collect it.

Broiler production across Africa varies enormously â from small-scale backyard operations in Malawi and Tanzania to semi-intensive units in Nigeria and commercial integrator farms in South Africa. Whatever your scale, the principle holds: health records are business records. A rising mortality figure is not just a veterinary concern; it is a cash-flow warning. A drop in feed intake is not just a husbandry note; it is a signal to recalculate your break-even price.

Why Benchmarks Matter in the African Context

In many African markets, broiler farmers sell live birds at local markets where price is negotiated per bird or per kilogram. Without a clear record of your cost per bird and your mortality rate, you cannot know whether a given price is profitable. The tables below provide reference figures drawn from published sources. Use them as guideposts, not gospel â your own farm records are the final authority.

One important caveat: African conditions vary widely. A farm in the highlands of Kenya may achieve feed conversion ratios closer to European standards, while a farm in the humid Niger Delta faces different disease pressure and heat stress. The benchmarks below represent achievable targets under good management, not guaranteed outcomes.

How to use this table: If your cumulative mortality at day 21 exceeds 2.5%, investigate immediately. If water intake drops by more than 10% from the previous day without a corresponding temperature change, suspect disease or water line failure. If FCR at day 35 exceeds 1.85, review feed quality, feed wastage, and flock health status.

Infectious bursal disease (Gumboro) 10â30% 10â30 (supportive care) 30â80 FAO (2013)
Poor water quality (bacterial load) 2â8% 5â20 (sanitisers, line cleaning) 10â30 MSD Animal Health (2021)

Note on figures: Costs are estimated in USD for illustration. Actual costs vary by country, feed price, and market price for live birds. The revenue loss column assumes a market price of USD 2.50â3.50 per kg live weight and a 2.5 kg bird at sale. Adjust to your local market. The purpose is to show that prevention (vaccination, biosecurity, water sanitation) is almost always cheaper than treatment and loss.

â  SAFETY WARNING â VETERINARY DRUGS AND VACCINES

Never administer veterinary drugs or vaccines without correct training and dosage guidance. Incorrect use can leave harmful residues in meat, harm the birds, and create antimicrobial resistance that affects human health. Always observe withdrawal periods before selling birds for slaughter. Store vaccines at the correct temperature (typically 2â8Â°C for most poultry vaccines) and never use expired products. If you are unsure, consult a qualified veterinarian or your local veterinary extension officer. In many African countries, only licensed veterinary professionals may legally prescribe certain antibiotics.

Source: WHO (2017), Guidelines on use of antimicrobials in food-producing animals; FAO (2013).

Decision Triggers: When to Act

The most valuable skill in broiler health management is knowing when a small problem is becoming a large one. The following decision triggers are practical thresholds based on the benchmarks above. When any trigger fires, act within 24 hours.

  • Mortality trigger: More than 0.5% mortality in a single day after day 7, or cumulative mortality exceeding the table above.
  • Water trigger: Water intake drops more than 10% from the previous day, or water:feed ratio falls below 1.5:1 after day 14.
  • Feed trigger: Feed intake drops more than 8% from the previous day, or FCR rises above the benchmark by more than 0.10.
  • Behaviour trigger: Birds huddling, panting excessively, or spreading away from each other in unusual patterns.
  • Financial trigger: Cost per kg live weight exceeds your expected selling price per kg for two consecutive days.

Each trigger should prompt a specific action: check water lines, review ventilation, inspect a sample of birds, and if the cause is not obvious within a few hours, call your veterinarian. In African markets where veterinary services may be distant, having a mobile phone contact for a vet or extension officer is as important as having feed in the store.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Record daily: mortality, feed consumed, water consumed, and any unusual behaviour â every single day, without exception.
  2. Calculate weekly: cumulative mortality %, FCR, and cost per kg live weight. Compare to the benchmarks in Table 1.
  3. Check water quality: test for bacterial load and sanitise drinker lines at least once per week.
  4. Verify vaccine cold chain: confirm fridge temperature is 2â8Â°C and that vaccines are not expired before use.
  5. Observe withdrawal periods: never sell birds for slaughter before the withdrawal period for any drug or vaccine has passed.
  6. Act on triggers: if any decision trigger fires, respond within 24 hours â do not wait for the next day.
  7. Keep a vet contact: have a named veterinarian or extension officer you can call, with their number stored in your phone.
  8. Review per batch: after each batch, compare your results to the previous batch and identify one thing to improve.

Further Reading

  • FAO (2013) â Good practices for biosecurity in the pig and poultry sectors â free PDF, covers disease prevention and farm-level biosecurity relevant to African smallholders.
  • Aviagen (2022) â Broiler Management Handbook â free PDF, includes performance objectives, water intake tables, and health monitoring guidance.
  • MSD Animal Health â Poultry Health Resources â free technical articles on vaccination, coccidiosis control, and water sanitation.
  • ILRI â African Chicken Genetic Gains â research on poultry health and productivity in African smallholder systems.
  • WHO (2017) â Guidelines on use of antimicrobials in food-producing animals â essential reading for responsible drug use and residue avoidance.

This reference lesson is designed to sit alongside your daily farm records. The tables and triggers are only useful if you actually write down what you see and compare it to what is expected. In broiler production, the farmer who records and reacts will consistently outperform the farmer who relies on memory and hope. Health is not just a veterinary matter â it is the foundation of your business.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the pre-starter diet in broiler production?
options: B) To support rapid early gut and immune development
D) To delay growth for uniformity
quiz.explanation: The pre-starter diet is formulated to support rapid development of the digestive tract and immune system during the first days of life.

quiz.q: At what age are broilers typically switched from starter to grower feed?
quiz.explanation: Broilers are usually transitioned from starter to grower feed around 10 to 14 days of age depending on the feeding program.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most critical for skeletal development in young broilers?
options: D) Vitamin C and vitamin K
quiz.explanation: Calcium and phosphorus are essential for bone formation and skeletal development in growing broilers.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum crude protein level in a typical broiler starter diet?
quiz.explanation: Broiler starter diets commonly contain around 22 to 24 percent crude protein to support rapid early growth.

quiz.q: Which feed form is generally associated with improved feed efficiency in broilers?
quiz.explanation: Pellets improve feed intake and feed efficiency by reducing sorting and increasing nutrient density per bite.

quiz.q: What is the main reason for adding fat to broiler diets?
quiz.explanation: Fat is added primarily to increase the energy density of the diet and support growth performance.

quiz.q: Which amino acid is typically the first limiting in corn-soy broiler diets?
quiz.explanation: Methionine is usually the first limiting amino acid in corn-soybean meal based broiler diets.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a withdrawal feed in broiler production?
options: D) To remove medication residues before slaughter
quiz.explanation: Withdrawal feed is used to ensure that medicated feed residues are cleared from the bird before processing.
